subject: botany_2
question_text: How can you differentiate between exonucleases and endonucleases?

insider_note: Ends against inside. The prefixes say it, and pointing that out is a good way to remember which is which.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Exonucleases
steps.margin_note: Where it cuts, what that means, and the prefix. Four lines.
lines: EXONUCLEASES cut DNA by removing nucleotides
from the ENDS of the molecule, one at a time.
They shorten the DNA but do not cut it in two.
steps.why: Working only from the ends means an exonuclease can trim a molecule but never divide it.
common_mistakes: Saying exonucleases cut within the DNA. They work from the ENDS.
Saying they cut DNA into fragments. They shorten it; they do not fragment it.
steps.memory_tip: EXO works from the ends, from the outside in.

steps.label: Endonucleases
steps.margin_note: Mirror the exo lines, then link to restriction enzymes.

lines.text: Exo trims the ends; endo cuts inside

lines: ENDONUCLEASES make cuts at specific positions
They cut the DNA into fragments.
steps.why: Only a cut made inside the molecule can produce two separate fragments, which is why genetic engineering uses endonucleases and not exonucleases.
common_mistakes: Saying endonucleases work from the ends. They cut WITHIN.

Describing only one of the two. The question asks for a difference, so both exonucleases and endonucleases must be described. Adding that restriction endonucleases are the ones used in genetic engineering is a good extra line.
steps.memory_tip: ENDO cuts inside, and that is the one used to make fragments.
